# Scientific method note

This task uses the scientific meaning of empirical dispersion corrections in
density-functional calculations and the package-independent data model used
by cclib. The note is a compact offline reference, not a copy of the upstream
bug report or its patch.

## Method evidence

The primary method reference is:

> S. Grimme, J. Antony, S. Ehrlich, H. Krieg, “A consistent and accurate ab
> initio parametrization of density functional dispersion correction (DFT-D)
> for the 94 elements H-Pu,” *The Journal of Chemical Physics* 132, 154104
> (2010). DOI: [10.1063/1.3382344](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.3382344).

The software/data-model reference is:

> N. M. O'Boyle et al., “cclib: A library for package-independent
> computational chemistry algorithms,” *Journal of Computational Chemistry*
> 29, 839-845 (2008). DOI:
> [10.1002/jcc.20823](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.20823).

The source snapshot contains the package's BSD-3-Clause license and its
documentation. The method paper and the source documentation are the
authoritative offline materials for this task.

## Energy meaning

An empirical dispersion model supplements a density-functional energy with a
signed pairwise contribution. In a simplified notation,

```text
E_method = E_base + E_pairwise
```

where the pairwise term is built from atom-pair coefficients, interatomic
distances, and a damping function. A representative form is

```text
E_pairwise = - sum(A < B) sum(n) s_n C_n(A,B) / R_AB^n * f_damp,n(R_AB)
```

The exact parameters and damping variants depend on the chosen method. The
important data contract is that the contribution is signed: a stabilizing
contribution is not an absolute magnitude that can be added with a guessed
sign. The terminal energy of the program and an earlier self-consistent-field
summary need not have the same physical meaning when the pairwise term is
reported in a later section.

## Parsing implications

The output of a quantum-chemistry program is a narrative record of a
calculation, not a single table. The same calculation can contain several
ordered energy records, and different versions or calculation modes can print
the base energy, the optional contribution, and the terminal result in
different sections. A package-independent parser therefore has two
responsibilities:

1. extract the scientific quantities represented in the supplied program
   family's supported output variants, keeping the contribution's sign and
   using the common unit convention documented by the package;
2. reconcile records that belong to the same calculation without silently
   changing ordinary calculations that have no optional contribution.

The canonical electronic-energy convention in this source snapshot is eV.
The output files themselves commonly print Hartree values as well, so a
conversion must be applied consistently rather than comparing numbers from
different unit systems. A multi-step calculation must preserve ordering: a
correction associated with one record must not be applied to a different
record merely because both values are finite.

## Offline investigation questions

When reading the supplied output, distinguish the following concepts rather
than matching a single number:

- an intermediate self-consistent-field energy;
- an optional signed pairwise correction;
- the terminal single-point energy emitted by the program;
- the normalized energy record returned by the common data model.

The paper does not identify a source filename or a patch. The source tree and
the output must be read together to determine where the package currently
loses the scientific relationship between these records.
